media.alt: Voluntary blood donations needed in Pakistan

content.text: "In Pakistan, less than 25 per cent of blood donations are voluntary and the supply of blood available in hospitals is far less than the demand from patients," said Dr Bushra Moiz, Consultant Haematologist, Aga Khan University Hospital at an event for World Blood Donor Day. This year's theme emphasises the need to improve the safety and sufficiency of blood supplies through 100 per cent voluntary unpaid donations. In countries like Pakistan that have still to reach this target, initiatives such as community blood drives and young people's involvement are needed to help phase out replacement donation, mainly from relatives, and do away with paid donation.

Even though globally 80 million units of blood are donated each year, in many parts of the world, people do not have access to safe blood when they need it. Voluntary blood donors are the safest blood source because they are the least likely to transmit infections and diseases like hepatitis and HIV/AIDS. Unfortunately, of all the blood donated from around the world, only 38 per cent comes from developing countries where 82 per cent of the world's population lives, and where the need is higher.

Dr Moiz was joined by Mr Hashim Hanif, Head of the Falah Organisation's Blood Bank and Mr Anwar Ajanee, Chairman of the Lions Club who spoke about the value of donating blood, as regular voluntary donors are the foundation of national blood programmes that can meet a country's requirements in routine and emergency situations. Many people are unaware of the fact that apart from possibly saving another person's life, donated blood is screened which alerts donors to the early signs of disease and can help them lead healthier lives.
